Python STABL parity: precisely what matches

Source: vignettes/stablr-python-parity.Rmd
stablr-python-parity.Rmd

1. Scope and source of the comparison

stablr is an R implementation of the STABL procedure described by Hédou et al. (2024). This vignette demonstrates the algorithmic parity that existing immutable Python-reference fixtures can support. It does not claim that R glmnet and Python scikit-learn yield identical fitted coefficients, or that a match to Python establishes universal false-discovery calibration.

The source-of-truth Python implementation is gregbellan/Stabl at commit 1d07f85a13cfbecb4f08ce21075bf4fbb8e34678, labeled 1.0.0 in the frozen fixture provenance. The frozen reference used Python 3.11.9, scikit-learn 1.3.2, numpy 1.26.4, and scipy 1.11.4. R reads packaged reference CSVs; Python is not required to build this article.

Canonical generator, input and integrity checks:

  • Fixture README
  • Fixture generator
  • Executable Python–R contract tests
  • Full-candidate release-evidence status
Comparison Evidence level Interpretation
Accumulation of frozen selection masks Exact numerical equality in unit tests Tests score bookkeeping, not fitted learner equivalence
FDP+ curve, selected threshold, strict-threshold support Exact up to numerical tolerance on frozen scores Tests algorithmic threshold semantics
Utility metrics and fixed stacking candidate selection Exact up to numerical tolerance in unit tests Tests shared algorithm inputs and tie conventions
Gaussian/binomial/multinomial LASSO; Gaussian elastic net Predeclared agreement thresholds for rankings/support Different optimization paths: not coefficient identity
Environmental aggregation, RF, ordinal, sPLS-DA, full multi-omic candidate workflow Not established by this vignette Require separate benchmark/validation evidence
Error-rate calibration on real or arbitrary null datasets Not established by parity Requires statistical assumptions and independent simulation evidence

2. Load the immutable reference scores

The package ships a small byte-for-byte subset of its canonical Python parity inputs in inst/extdata/python_parity_vignette. These are copied from, not substituted for, the original frozen test fixtures. Every file is included in a SHA-256 manifest in the accompanying source bundle.

library(stablr)
fixture_dir <- system.file("extdata", "python_parity_vignette", package = "stablr")
stopifnot(nzchar(fixture_dir))
read_fixture <- function(name) {
  utils::read.csv(file.path(fixture_dir, name), check.names = FALSE,
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
scores <- read_fixture("stability_scores.csv")
curve <- read_fixture("fdp_plus_curve.csv")
reference <- read_fixture("stabl_fit_reference.csv")

score_matrix <- function(kind) {
  subset_scores <- scores[scores$feature_type == kind, , drop = FALSE]
  {
    features <- unique(subset_scores$feature)
    lambdas <- unique(subset_scores$lambda_id)
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, length(features), length(lambdas),
                  dimnames = list(features, lambdas))
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(subset_scores))) {
      out[subset_scores$feature[i], subset_scores$lambda_id[i]] <-
        subset_scores$stability_score[i]
    }
    stopifnot(!anyNA(out))
    out
  }
}
real_scores <- score_matrix("real")
artificial_scores <- score_matrix("artificial")
stopifnot(nrow(real_scores) == 8L, nrow(artificial_scores) == 4L)

3. Reproduce Python’s FDP+ diagnostic exactly

With the identical stability scores, candidate thresholds and artificial-to-original feature proportion, the R implementation reproduces the pinned Python FDP+ curve and the first minimum of that curve. In this fixture the minimum is attained at both 0.25 and 0.375; the first-minimum policy selects 0.25.

observed <- compute_fdp_plus(
  stabl_scores = real_scores,
  stabl_scores_artificial = artificial_scores,
  artificial_proportion = 0.5,
  fdr_threshold_range = curve$threshold
)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(unname(observed$FDRs), curve$fdp_plus,
                   tolerance = 1e-12)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(observed$min_fdr, min(curve$fdp_plus),
                   tolerance = 1e-12))
)
first_min <- curve$threshold[curve$is_first_minimum == 1L]
stopifnot(length(first_min) == 1L)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(observed$fdr_min_threshold,
                           first_min, tolerance = 1e-12)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  property = c("Minimum FDP+", "Chosen stability threshold",
               "Number of tied minima"),
  value = c(format(observed$min_fdr, digits = 5),
            format(observed$fdr_min_threshold, digits = 5),
            as.character(sum(curve$fdp_plus == min(curve$fdp_plus))))
))
property value
Minimum FDP+ 0.25
Chosen stability threshold 0.25
Number of tied minima 2 
plot(curve$threshold, curve$fdp_plus, type = "b", pch = 16,
     xlab = "Candidate stability-score threshold",
     ylab = "FDP+ diagnostic (not realized FDP)")
abline(v = observed$fdr_min_threshold, lty = 2)
points(observed$fdr_min_threshold, observed$min_fdr, pch = 19, cex = 1.5)

Pinned Python-reference FDP+ curve. The dotted vertical line marks the first minimum, not a guaranteed false-discovery rate.

4. Reproduce selected-feature support and tie policy

The reference uses strict >: a feature with a maximum score equal to the chosen threshold is not selected. In this pinned example gene_e has score 0.25 and is therefore excluded, while gene_d has 0.5 and is selected. Strict-vs-inclusive comparisons are a documented methodological decision; this vignette preserves reference behavior rather than silently switching it.

maximum <- apply(real_scores, 1L, max)
r_selected <- as.integer(maximum[reference$feature] > observed$fdr_min_threshold)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(unname(maximum[reference$feature]),
                   reference$max_stability_score, tolerance = 1e-12)),
  identical(r_selected, reference$selected)
)
knitr::kable(data.frame(feature = reference$feature,
                        python_score = reference$max_stability_score,
                        python_selected = as.logical(reference$selected),
                        r_selected = as.logical(r_selected)))
feature python_score python_selected r_selected
signal_a 1.000 TRUE TRUE
signal_b 0.875 TRUE TRUE
gene_c 0.625 TRUE TRUE
gene_d 0.500 TRUE TRUE
gene_e 0.250 FALSE FALSE
noise_f 0.250 FALSE FALSE
noise_g 0.125 FALSE FALSE
noise_h 0.000 FALSE FALSE

5. Solver-level parity is a different, tolerance-based contract

A separate test suite performs R glmnet fits using the same predictor matrix, responses and prescribed bootstrap sample IDs as the pinned Python scikit-learn baseline. These are not comparisons of automatically generated R and Python lambda paths. The frozen benchmark’s acceptance limits are:

gates <- read_fixture("solver_cases.csv")
knitr::kable(gates[, c("case", "spearman_min", "top5_overlap_min", "jaccard_min")],
             digits = 2)
case spearman_min top5_overlap_min jaccard_min
gaussian_lasso 0.8 4 0.6
binomial_lasso 0.8 4 0.6
multinomial_lasso 0.7 3 0.5
gaussian_elastic_net 0.7 3 0.5

These numbers are minimum acceptance gates, not observed agreement statistics. Do not label this table “Python–R achieved concordance”. The achieved comparison is not displayed in this miniature vignette. It is computed and asserted by test-python-parity-fixtures.R against the full pinned solver_* fixtures; that test must pass in CI. Since coefficient penalties differ between scikit-learn and glmnet, an equivalent fitted model can require explicit parameter mapping (e.g., Python C versus R lambda), intercept and normalization conventions. Do not imply byte-identical coefficients or random-number streams.

6. What the two plots mean

The stability path plots how frequently each feature is selected across bootstrap subsamples at each lambda/learner setting. High curves indicate repeated algorithmic selection, not biological truth. Sparse/dense directions depend on the chosen learner/grid and must be checked from the axis labels.

The FDP+ curve plots a decoy-based diagnostic against candidate stability cut-offs. A minimum chooses a cut-off under the published STABL procedure; a lower minimum is not automatically a controlled FDR, and a curve value greater than 1 can occur because FDP+ is an estimator, not a probability. Near-zero artificial-score separation, a flat minimum or selection saturation warrants caution. An empty support is legitimate and should not be silently replaced by top-ranked features.

For a compact illustrated walkthrough, see vignette("stablr-reading-plots") after installing the accompanying page.

7. Reproduction boundaries

  • The installed vignette has no Python dependency, because it reads frozen CSV evidence.
  • To regenerate canonical fixtures, use the pinned Python checkout, explicit environment, generator and SHA-256 verification steps in the fixture README.
  • Passing parity means matching a specified reference contract. It does not show that STABL’s selected set has a calibrated realized false-discovery proportion in every empirical regime. See the adversarial scientific findings.
  • The separately governed full OOL candidate run historically failed its 0.1.1 parity gates; this page must not be cited as evidence that the later full-candidate release gate has passed.

References: Hédou J, et al. Nature Biotechnology (2024), DOI 10.1038/s41587-023-02033-x; original Python STABL repository.
